events.title: Hackers raised freezer temperature at Selver supermarket to +50°C

articles.text: News ERR {{1793612640000 | amCalendar}} Updated: {{1793621580000 | amCalendar}} share Facebook X (Twitter) e-mail Refrigerated products at a supermarket in Estonia (photo is illustrative). Source: Priit Mürk/ERR News A cyber attack hit a Selver supermarket in Estonia, with hackers accessing a computer controlling refrigeration and changing a freezer setting to 50 degrees above zero. Similar incidents were reported on Monday in Sweden, Belgium and Luxembourg. Jann Mutso, head of refrigeration technology maker and distributor Kitman Coldtech, told ERR that one of its clients was attacked, but that there had been other attacks. "I don't know exactly yet, but other clients in Estonia have also been attacked, not only ours. This is very fresh, it happened this morning," Mutso said. Selver communications chief Mariann Järvela said the attack took place in one Selver outlet. "For security reasons we will not disclose more specific information about the particular store or the technical solutions," Järvela added. She said the chain was aware of similar cyber attacks elsewhere in the world and had therefore prepared for possible threats. The partner identified the attack quickly and the store suffered no damage. Järvela said they pay great attention to the security of technical systems and have consistently updated the controllers and software solutions of stores' refrigeration systems. "This was the last Selver store where the new system had not yet been taken into use," Järvela said. According to Mutso, the attackers gained access to the control computer of an older type of Danfoss refrigeration system and raised its temperature to 50 degrees. The method resembles attacks in France and the Netherlands in October, where the operation of supermarkets' digital refrigeration systems was also interfered with and their temperature settings changed. "The signature is the same, but I can't comment further yet," Mutso said. He said it is normal in large food stores for refrigeration systems to be digital and connected to the network, but that the current attack sought specific security holes. "All the store chains have started fighting this and have updated their controllers, but there are also places where the controllers are old and not updated, and those are being targeted now," the refrigeration systems maker said. This time the incident was responded to within ten minutes, and so damage was avoided. Mutso said the temperature in the freezers rose by about two to three degrees and no damage was caused to products, with normal temperature restored in about 10–15 minutes. How the attackers gained access is not yet known. Attacks also occurred in other European countries Similar attacks hit food stores in Belgium, Luxembourg and Sweden. Swedish daily Dagens Nyheter reported overnight faults in the refrigeration systems of ICA and Coop stores. "The worst-case scenario has come true," the ICA store in Sjöbo said on social media, after its freezers were set to 50 degrees and spoiled goods had to be pulled from sale. Engla Ingwall, sales manager at ICA Baronen in Stockholm, said freezers became "extremely hot" and a significant quantity of food was thrown away. Police were informed. An ICA spokesperson said the number of affected stores is small and involves those with connections outside the central network. Coop said six of its central Swedish stores were affected, and new systems had already been ordered after the French incident. According to Reuters, supermarket chain Ahold Delhaize identified temperature rises in its fridges and freezers in Belgium and Luxembourg and is investigating. Belgian outlet Le Soir reported problems in several Shop&Go and Carrefour stores. About three weeks ago, hundreds of food stores in France were hacked, with attackers triggering a defrost cycle in many stores of major retail chains. Neither ICA nor Coop has yet confirmed whether hackers were behind Monday's issues in Sweden. Editor's note: This piece was updated to include comment from Selver and information on the Europe-wide hacking. -- Follow ERR News on Facebook and Twitter and never miss an update! events.title: Russia's statistics agency confirms cyberattack claimed by Belarusian and Ukrainian hackers

articles.text: The hacking groups claimed to have left this message on the servers of Russia's statistics agency. Russia's statistics agency confirms cyberattack claimed by Belarusian and Ukrainian hackers An alliance of Belarusian and pro-Ukrainian hackers claimed to have taken out Russia's federal statistics agency, Rosstat, and stolen vast amounts of sensitive government data in a cyberattack over the weekend. The Belarusian Cyber Partisans and the pro-Ukrainian hacking group Silent Crow said Sunday they spent months inside Rosstat's network before launching a destructive operation that wiped servers and disrupted the agency's systems. Rosstat confirmed that it had been targeted by a cyberattack but disputed the hackers' claims about the extent of the breach, saying it had found no evidence that protected information had been leaked or its databases compromised. In a statement to Russian state news agency TASS, Rosstat said its security systems had detected suspicious activity in time for specialists to respond. The agency said it was working with cybersecurity experts and law enforcement to identify the source of the attacks. Rosstat, which collects and publishes official statistics on Russia's population, economy and social conditions, holds extensive government data, including demographic records and information from Russian-occupied Ukrainian territories. According to the Cyber Partisans, the hackers first gained access to Rosstat's network about six months ago and spent the following four months quietly moving through its systems, collecting internal documents and expanding their access. "We reached the agency's critical systems while systematically extracting sensitive data and internal documents," the group claimed. The hackers said they began preparing for the destructive phase of the operation about a month ago, with the most intensive activity taking place over the past two weeks. The attack culminated overnight on Saturday, they said, with the destruction of physical and virtual servers, along with large-scale data storage systems. Silent Crow claimed the operation gave the hackers access to approximately 25,000 computers and other devices across Rosstat's headquarters, regional offices and main statistical data processing center. The group purported to have compromised systems used to manage the agency's network, including domain controllers, virtualization platforms and infrastructure management tools. The hackers also said they breached databases containing economic, demographic and personal information, census records and internal government correspondence. Among the allegedly stolen material were confidential mortality records detailing causes of death in Russia, as well as nonpublic statistics from Russian-occupied Ukrainian territories. The groups also claimed to have obtained information about Russian military casualties in the war against Ukraine. The hackers' claims about the scale of the breach, the destruction of infrastructure and the theft of sensitive data could not be independently verified. The Cyber Partisans said they planned to release a detailed account of the operation, along with samples of the allegedly stolen data, in the coming days. The groups also claimed to have replaced content on Rosstat's servers with official Ukrainian statistics on Russian military losses. They said the information remained publicly accessible for about an hour before the agency's systems began experiencing disruptions. Russian newspaper Kommersant reported that hackers had defaced Rosstat's main website and regional portals, leaving messages that included a warning in Belarusian: "No one will escape accountability." A familiar alliance This was not the first time the two hacking groups have joined forces to target major Russian organizations. In July 2025, the Cyber Partisans and Silent Crow claimed responsibility for a disruptive cyberattack on Aeroflot, Russia's flagship airline, which forced the carrier to cancel more than 100 flights and affected roughly 20,000 passengers. The hackers claimed to have destroyed parts of the airline's IT infrastructure and stolen sensitive information, including flight records, internal communications and employee monitoring data. They later published what they said were flight records belonging to Aeroflot's chief executive. The Cyber Partisans said Rosstat had proven to be a more difficult target than the airline. "Unlike Aeroflot, which we attacked in 2025, Rosstat had a more robust security system," the group said. The Belarusian Cyber Partisans emerged following mass protests against President Alexander Lukashenko in 2020, after an election widely condemned by Western governments as fraudulent. The group has since carried out cyber operations targeting Belarusian and Russian government institutions. In October, the group disclosed that it had infiltrated Moscow's healthcare network in 2023, claiming to have gained administrator-level access to systems connected to other government agencies. Silent Crow has also claimed responsibility for attacks on Russian government agencies and businesses, including an earlier breach of Rosreestr, the country's state property registry. In July, Russia's Supreme Court designated both hacking groups as extremist organizations, effectively outlawing their activities in the country and exposing individuals associated with them to potential criminal prosecution. The practical consequences of the designation remain unclear, as the hackers have continued targeting Russian organizations. "It looks like Rosstat will have to recalculate not only its statistics this time, but also the scale of its own problems," Silent Crow said. News Cybercrime No previous article No new articles Daryna Antoniuk is a reporter for Recorded Future News based in Ukraine. She writes about cybersecurity startups, cyberattacks in Eastern Europe and the state of the cyberwar between Ukraine and Russia. She previously was a tech reporter for Forbes Ukraine. Her work has also been published at Sifted, The Kyiv Independent and The Kyiv Post.
